historical_timeline.summary: Heart attack while teaching tennis to young people.
Second (double) bypass operation, with a blood transfusion.

claims.statement: Arthur Robert Ashe Jr. was born in Richmond, Virginia, on July 10, 1943, to Mattie Cunningham Ashe and Arthur Robert Ashe Sr.; his mother died before he was seven.
On July 31, 1979, while teaching tennis to inner-city youth, Ashe had a heart attack, and he then underwent quadruple coronary artery bypass surgery in 1979.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic coronary artery disease and old myocardial infarction. One source dates a first heart attack to July 1976; the 1979 date is preferred (see sources.md).

source_links.locator: dates his first heart attack to July 1976

claims.statement: When chest pain recurred, Ashe had a second bypass operation, a double bypass, in 1983, during which he received a blood transfusion.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for two bypass operations.

claims.statement: In 1988 Ashe had difficulty moving his right hand and arm; a scan showed a mass in the left side of his brain, which surgeons removed, and the diagnosis was toxoplasmosis. Testing then showed that he had HIV and AIDS.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic HIV disease with a history of cerebral toxoplasmosis. The month of the operation was not verified in a fetched source.

source_links.locator: emergency brain surgery after experiencing paralysis of his right arm

claims.statement: Ashe and his doctors concluded that he had almost certainly acquired HIV from a blood transfusion during his 1983 heart operation, before blood was tested for the virus.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents the route of acquisition; the modern frame keeps it as history only (see sources.md).

claims.statement: Ashe kept his diagnosis private at first, telling only a few family members and friends. On April 8, 1992, after learning that USA Today planned to report it, he announced at a press conference that he had HIV.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the true-frame index date; recorded in the timeline. Supports the episode's emphasis on his control over disclosure.

claims.statement: Both of Ashe's parents had atherosclerotic heart disease at early ages. His mother died at 27 of complications from surgery, and his father had two heart attacks, at 55 and at 59.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history of early coronary disease.

claims.statement: Ashe died in New York City on February 6, 1993, aged 49, of AIDS-related pneumonia. His memoir, Days of Grace, was published after his death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a fact without detail; after the episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Person-first, confidential primary care for a 45-year-old man four months after HIV was diagnosed with cerebral toxoplasmosis, who also has coronary artery disease after two bypass operations: viral load and CD4 monitoring on bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide (an antiretroviral regimen chosen to avoid interactions with his statin and cardiac medicines and to avoid abacavir), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole maintenance and its safe discontinuation by CD4 count, vaccines for adults with HIV, and secondary prevention of coronary disease to an LDL goal below 55 mg/dL, on the DHHS and IAS-USA antiretroviral guidance, the DHHS opportunistic infection guidelines, the HIVMA/IDSA primary care guidance, and the CMID ischemic heart disease and hyperlipidemia monographs.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Ashe returns four weeks after his first visit and is seen by Dr. Rao of infectious diseases on the same day. He takes bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide each morning and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole twice a day, and has missed no doses. He started ezetimibe four weeks ago without muscle aches. He has had no headache, seizure, or weakness, and his right hand feels normal. He has had no rash, fever, cough, or breathlessness, and no chest pain. He is sleeping better than at the first visit and has started to coach again two afternoons a week. He has told no one new about his diagnosis and asked again that his results go only to him.

referral.question: HIV infection diagnosed four months ago with cerebral toxoplasmosis and a CD4 count of 58, in a 45-year-old man who also has coronary artery disease after two bypass operations. Please review his antiretroviral regimen and its interactions with his cardiac medicines, and advise on opportunistic-infection prophylaxis, the monitoring schedule, and vaccines, so that we can co-manage his care
referral.urgency: Routine, within four weeks, on the same day as his four-week primary care visit
referral.pertinent_history: Admitted four months ago with right-hand weakness; MRI showed a single ring-enhancing left frontoparietal lesion, and stereotactic biopsy showed Toxoplasma. HIV was diagnosed during that admission, with a viral load of 186,000 copies/mL and a CD4 count of 58. The genotype showed no resistance mutations; hepatitis B surface antigen, surface antibody, and core antibody were negative; hepatitis C antibody negative; hepatitis A antibody positive; interferon-gamma release assay negative; Toxoplasma IgG positive. He completed six weeks of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin, and has taken trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength twice daily since. Bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide were started two weeks into toxoplasmosis treatment. His right hand has recovered. Today, after about 15 weeks of therapy: viral load 42 copies/mL, CD4 156, hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, potassium 4.9 mmol/L, creatinine 1.18 mg/dL (0.98 before treatment), ALT 30, LDL 88 mg/dL. Coronary disease: myocardial infarction at 36, quadruple bypass the same year, and a double bypass for recurrent angina at 39, with a blood transfusion during that operation; no angina now. He takes aspirin 81 mg and atorvastatin 80 mg, ezetimibe was added today, and he has sublingual nitroglycerin. PCV20, a first hepatitis B vaccine dose, and a first meningococcal ACWY dose were given today. He has asked that his diagnosis and results be shared with no one without his consent

consultant_note.history: Mr. Ashe, a 45-year-old man, is seen at the request of Dr. Tolliver for co-management of HIV. HIV was diagnosed four months ago when he presented with right-hand weakness from cerebral toxoplasmosis, confirmed by stereotactic biopsy; the CD4 count was 58 and the viral load 186,000 copies/mL. He completed six weeks of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and leucovorin and has taken trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength twice daily since. He started bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide two weeks into toxoplasmosis treatment and has missed no doses. He has had no headache, seizure, fever, rash, or cough, and his right hand has recovered. He acquired HIV, he understands, from a blood transfusion during his second bypass operation; the hospital reported the suspected transfusion-transmitted infection to the blood supplier at diagnosis. He has coronary artery disease after two bypass operations and has no angina. He is clear that he alone decides who learns of his diagnosis
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Hospital records, including the MRI, the biopsy report, the baseline genotype, and the hepatitis, tuberculosis, and Toxoplasma serologies. Dr. Tolliver's intake note four weeks ago, with the viral load (42 copies/mL), CD4 count (156), blood count, metabolic panel, ALT, lipid panel, and ECG. Today's metabolic panel, below

exam.finding: Well and composed; weight 72.6 kg; blood pressure 116/72
No thrush or oral hairy leukoplakia
No enlarged nodes
No rash
Grip strength and fine finger movements equal on both sides; no focal deficit

assessment.assessment: Responding well: the viral load has fallen from 186,000 to 42 copies/mL in about 15 weeks and should become undetectable within the next few months, and the CD4 count has risen from 58 to 156. Bictegravir with emtricitabine and tenofovir alafenamide is a recommended first regimen, has a high barrier to resistance, and has no meaningful interaction with aspirin, atorvastatin, ezetimibe, or nitroglycerin. A regimen boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat would raise atorvastatin levels and limit its dose, efavirenz would lower them, and abacavir has been associated with myocardial infarction and should be avoided in a man with coronary disease

Clinically resolved. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength twice daily is an accepted maintenance regimen and also prevents Pneumocystis pneumonia. It can stop once the CD4 count has been above 200 for more than six months on ART with a suppressed viral load, provided he remains free of symptoms. Prophylaxis for Mycobacterium avium complex is not needed, because he started fully active ART promptly

The rise from 0.98 to about 1.17 mg/dL is expected and stable. Both bictegravir and trimethoprim block tubular secretion of creatinine without lowering the true filtration rate. Potassium is high-normal on trimethoprim and should be watched

Inactivated vaccines can be given at any CD4 count, although responses are better as the count recovers. Live vaccines are contraindicated while the CD4 count is below 200; he is immune to measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella and needs none

HIV raises cardiovascular risk independently, which strengthens rather than changes the secondary-prevention plan: high-intensity atorvastatin with ezetimibe to an LDL below 55 mg/dL, aspirin, and blood pressure below 130/80. Integrase inhibitors can cause weight gain, which should be tracked

recommendations: Continue bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide once daily; take it two hours before or six hours after any antacid, calcium, iron, or magnesium
Avoid abacavir, ritonavir- or cobicistat-boosted regimens, and efavirenz; check any new medicine for interactions with the HIV regimen and with atorvastatin

Continue trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength twice daily; stop it when the CD4 count has been above 200 for more than six months with an undetectable viral load and no symptoms, and restart it if the count falls below 200
Viral load and CD4 count every three months until the CD4 count is stably above 200 and prophylaxis has stopped, then every three to six months

Blood count, potassium, and creatinine every three months while on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; ALT every six months; lipids per the coronary plan; urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio with the three-month blood tests and then yearly on tenofovir alafenamide, as it was not done at the start of therapy

Second hepatitis B vaccine dose today and a surface antibody check one to two months later; second meningococcal ACWY dose at least eight weeks after the first; recombinant zoster vaccine, two doses; influenza and COVID-19 vaccines each autumn; no live vaccines
Keep atorvastatin 80 mg and the ezetimibe added today, with an LDL goal below 55 mg/dL; track weight on the integrase inhibitor
Anal cancer screening and colorectal cancer screening from age 45, at his preventive visit
Share results with him alone, by secure message, unless he asks otherwise; peer support and counseling are available when he wants them
